Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa

The Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa is a sovereign Ojibwe government whose homeplace is Grand Portage on Lake Superior. Its government page identifies its 1854 treaty relationship and membership in the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe. A Band land-return release and the National Park Service’s place-specific interpretation offer a starting path through homeland, land tenure and the portage corridor.

01

Gichi Onigaming and a living homeplace

The National Park Service identifies Grand Portage National Monument as within the homeland of the Grand Portage Anishinaabe and the community as the Band’s homeplace and governmental center. It explains Gichi Onigaming as the carrying place connecting Lake Superior and the continent’s interior, and records the Band’s donation of approximately half the monument’s land. Read that interpretation with the Band’s own government statement. The reconstructed lakeshore depot pictured here is a public interpretation site within this homeplace; it is not a surviving eighteenth-century village or a portrait of the whole community.

Read the sources [3] National Park Service [1] Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa

02

A dated account of land return

A March 2026 Band release reports the return of three parcels, totaling about 87 acres, through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. It describes three different routes by which those particular parcels left Band ownership: treaty cession, state school-trust transfer and allotment. This is a direct community account of one land acquisition and its historical meaning. The release usefully distinguishes mechanisms of land loss, while the underlying titles, allotment documents and treaty instruments remain separate research tasks. It does not define the full extent of Grand Portage homeland.

Government — Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa ↗

Publication: Current election information for 2026; historical statement undated

The Band states its inherent sovereignty, its 1854 treaty relationship and membership in the six-band Minnesota Chippewa Tribe. This concise government page is useful for direct identity and present-governance context; detailed historical claims are supported by the NPS history page and treaties.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Read the page’s complete main government statement (lines 12–31). Counts as supporting context only.

Tribal news release / contemporary land stewardshipGrand Portage Band of Lake Superior ChippewaSource 2

Grand Portage Band Regains Historic Tribal Land ↗

Publication: March 16, 2026

A Grand Portage Band news release reports that a February 2026 acquisition restored three parcels totaling about 87 acres to Band ownership through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. The Band describes three distinct routes by which those parcels left Band ownership: 1854 treaty cession, state school-trust transfer, and allotment. This is a direct community source for the Bands current action and its historical interpretation; the underlying treaty, land-title chain, tax records, and allotment documents were not independently checked. The Bands broad discussion of allotment policy remains attributed to the release and is not generalized to every Ojibwe Band. A linked map/images package is not included.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the full 83-line public Band news release on October 23, 2026. It reports the February 16, 2026 acquisition of three parcels through a Band/Foundation partnership, describes the Band account of different land-loss mechanisms, and quotes the Band chair and partner representatives. Its linked map/images were not opened or used. The Band statements about federal policy and the parcels past ownership are attributed community interpretation; underlying treaty, land-title and allotment records were not independently inspected.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

History & Culture — Grand Portage National Monument ↗

Publication: Updated 2026-01-23

The park identifies Grand Portage National Monument as within the homeland of the Grand Portage Anishinaabe and identifies the Band as the center of tribal government. It describes the portage corridor and Minong (Isle Royale) as important to Grand Portage. This park interpretation is geographically specific and does not define all Ojibwe homelands.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete History & Culture page, especially lines 22–52 on Gichi Onigaming, trade, Grand Portage homeland, land donation and Minong. Linked articles and image files were not opened.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026
